To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the refrigerant end temperatures associated with isentropic compressions can be reduced by up to 10%, but the volumetric efficiencies of vapour compression systems can be reduced by as much as 7%.
real gas effects play both a favourable and unfavourable role during the isothermal compression process.
the gas compressibilty effect is a favourable one during the isentrofic compression process and an unfavourable one during the isobaric expansion process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the gas compressibilities of refrigerants and their mixtures.
the analysis of the thermodynamic effects which occur during the isentrope processes of refrigerants (and refrigerant mixtures) in the vapour phase.
the analysis of the real gas effects during the isentropes of ideal vapour-compression cycles, which take place within work transfer components of the cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the considered refrigerants, real gas effects can reduce the cooling (or the heating) capacity of a vapour compression system, but they can also reduce the compressor work and the corresponding electrical power demand.
the real gas effects are ‘favourable’, but only in part.
the refrigerant gas compressibility effects are ‘neutral’ for the ideal vapour compression cycle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the real gas effects should be taken into account in order to properly analyse the thermodynamic performance of the work transfer components in vapour compression cycles.
the refrigerant end temperatures are higher and the work transferred is lower for the real gas modelling than the ideal gas modelling.

, in the vapour compression cycles, the refrigerant compressibility effects are ‘beneficial’ for the refrigerant end-temperature, but they are ‘unfavourably’ related to the volumetric efficiency of the compressor and, consequently, to the cooling (or the heating) capacity of refrigerating (or heating) equipment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for the first time in the literature, a real gas model has been developed for refrigerant mixtures, and that it has been used to calculate the thermodynamic properties of pure and mixed refrigerant vapours during the isentropics of vapour compression cycles.
the real gas effects should be carefully taken into account in order to properly design vapour compression systems.

the real gas modelling is necessary to accurately predict the thermodynamic properties of refrigerants and their mixtures in the vapour phase and, consequently, to correctly assess the refrigerating (or heating) power and the work exchanged in a vapour compression cycle.
